title: lock-contention-tokenizer-sampling-wip
content:
Purpose:
This note documents a focused investigation into CPU-side contention observed in the hosted serving runtime where short requests (<=64 tokens) show unexpectedly high tail latency. Hypothesis: tokenizer and small-request parsing path are suffering lock contention / GIL-related stalls inside the thread pool, amplified by work-stealing and frequent tiny allocations.

Background/context:
- Symptom: p95/p99 tail latency spikes on small (chat) requests during steady-state throughput (50–120 rps per instance).
- Affected endpoints: /v1/chat/stream and /v1/completions when request payloads include client-side system messages and multi-turn context.
- Prior work: we have microprofiler snapshots and aggregated `py-spy` traces (see linked S3 profile). This doc attempts to synthesize sampling + perf + userland instrumentation to identify concrete mitigations.

Hardware and test harness:
- Instance: c6a-like equivalent, 32 vCPU, 128 GB RAM, Linux 6.x kernel (customer-like host).
- Runtime image: rwd-inference/serving:release-2026-01-27 (Python 3.11, tokenizers via tiktoken fork).
- Load: 100 rps steady, payload distribution skewed to short contexts (median 18 tokens).
- Measurement tools: `perf record -F 99 -g`, `perf script` + FlameGraph, `py-spy record --native`, `eBPF off-CPU` stack sampling (bcc `offcputime.py`), and our in-process microprofiler (instrumentation hooks around tokenization + parse + request pipeline).

Methodology (what we measured):
1) Wall-clock sampling across stacks (perf + py-spy) over 120s windows during spike reproduction.
2) eBPF off-CPU to capture time spent waiting on futexes/mutexes and syscalls.
3) Microbenchmarks: single-threaded tokenization runs (100k short strings) to measure median allocations and time per call.
4) Thread-pool saturation tests: vary pool size and enable/disable work-stealing to observe queueing and context switch behavior.
5) Compare tiktoken fork vs pure Python fallback for a subset of tokens to check C-extension behavior.

Key observations (raw):
- Tokenization accounted for ~28% of sampled CPU time on tail traces; request parsing (JSON -> internal objects) ~14%; GIL/syscall related wait ~18% (futex wait stacks present in off-CPU traces).
- High number of short-lived Python frames in the stacks (~15–25 frames deep) pointing to allocation churn (object creation in parse/tokenize path).
- Thread-pool worker stacks often show `PyThread_acquire_lock` and `futex_wait` sequences during peak, suggesting workers blocked on a mutex (notably: dynamic vocabulary cache and shared tokenizer state).
- Enabling work-stealing reduced median latency slightly but increased context switches and exacerbated futex waits (more cross-thread wakeups).
- C-extension tokenizer variants (shared C tokenizers) showed lower CPU per request but higher lock contention when using a shared internal char->token cache protected by a global lock.

Representative perf samples (aggregated):
- 28.4% tokenization functions (split among tokenizer.c::encode, tokenizer.c::norm, python wrapper frames)
- 18.1% futex/lock wait stacks (off-CPU)
- 13.7% JSON parsing & request building (python json.loads + dataclass ctor overhead)
- 8.9% GC and short-lived object collection (alloc/free churn measured via tracemalloc)
- remainder: syscall overhead, user code (handler), networking stack (small)

Evidence and artifacts:
- Flamegraph: s3://redwood-profiles/2026-01/tokenizer-locking/flamegraph.svg (see `tokenizer.encode` cluster and adjacent `PyThread_acquire_lock`).
- eBPF off-CPU: avg futex wait time per stall event ~350us, with spikes to 2.1ms at p99.
- py-spy: captured many GIL-bound Python frames where native C wrappers call back into Python for encoding pre/post hooks.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Shared tokenizer caches (vocab maps, BPE merges cache) are protected by a coarse global lock — contention increases with number of workers for small requests.
2) Work-stealing causes more cross-thread notifications/wakes which interact poorly with Python's futex/backing kernel primitives, increasing scheduling overhead for tiny workloads.
3) JSON parsing allocates temporary objects that compete with tokenization for the same allocator/GC cycles, causing short GC pauses impacting tail latency.
4) The C-extension wrapper sometimes reacquires the GIL for callbacks into pure-Python normalization hooks; these reacquisitions cause short stop-the-world stalls at scale.

Quick experiments and results tried so far:
- Experiment A: Replace global tokenizer cache with thread-local caches (per-worker LRU, TTL 5s). Result: tokenization CPU dropped ~12% on short-request traces; futex waits reduced by ~9%; overall p99 improved by ~7%.
- Experiment B: Disable work-stealing in the thread pool (affinity: fixed-to-core mapping). Result: median latency stable, p95 improved slightly but p99 worsened for bursts — indicates benefits for steady small loads but poorer burst handling.
- Experiment C: Swap JSON parser from `json` to `orjson` in the critical path. Result: request parse CPU fell by ~6% and allocations decreased; small improvement in tail but not sufficient alone.
- Experiment D: Build tokenizer C-extension variant without global cache (pure C, per-thread caches). Result: best CPU profile but introduced memory regression (~2.2× peak mem) due to per-thread duplication; acceptable for some Dedicated customers but not for hosted with multi-tenancy.

Actionable recommendations (short-term):
- Patch 1 (low-risk): introduce worker-local soft caches for tokenizer internals (LRU + sampling TTL). Roll out behind feature flag and monitor futex wait and p99 latency. Create feature flag `tokenizer.local_cache`.
- Patch 2 (mid-risk): remove Python callbacks from C-extension fast path; perform normalization in Python pre-encode step (batch normalization) to reduce GIL reacquisitions inside C wrapper. Requires validating tokenization parity with existing models.
- Patch 3 (ops): increase thread pool worker CPUs affinity tuning for short-request tiers to limit cross-socket wakeups and reduce unnecessary context switches in noisy neighbors. Add monitoring metric `worker.futex_wait_us`.
- Patch 4 (experimental): evaluate a per-request tokenization queue that batches short tokenization calls in micro-batches (10 ms window) to amortize lock acquisition and reduce syscalls — measure impact on added latency.

Risks and tradeoffs:
- Per-thread caches reduce lock contention but increase memory footprint; need budgeting per deployment type (Hosted vs Dedicated).
- Removing callbacks from C-extension can reduce flexibility (fewer post-hooks for logging/metrics) and requires careful regression tests on tokenization outputs.
- Batching tokenization adds complexity and may hurt single-request latency for rare flows (must be optional).

Open questions / TODOs:
- [ ] Quantify memory impact of per-thread caches across the fleet (simulate median tenancies).
- [ ] Add synthetic regression test to ensure tokenization parity post-change (unit tests + fuzzing on corner cases).
- [ ] Wire up a futex-wait dashboard (histograms, p50/p95/p99) in the Console so we can see rollouts impact in real-time.
- [ ] Measure the effect of Python 3.12-specific allocator improvements (can we test with 3.12 beta image?)

Next steps (owners & tickets):
- Maya: push prototype of worker-local cache behind flag (GH#2683) — due 2026-02-20. Ticket CON-1423.
- Arjun: run memory simulation for per-thread caches on staging (script: tools/mem-sim.py) — due 2026-02-25.
- Leah: add futex wait and off-CPU dashboards to Console (Metric: `serving.worker.futex.wait_us`) — due 2026-02-28.
- Tomás: run single-node benchmark comparing batch-tokenize micro-batcher vs baseline and report CPU/latency tradeoffs — due 2026-03-04.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally light on final numbers because we re-ran different variants during the week; please refer to the S3 profile and GH PR for exact flamegraphs and raw `perf` outputs. The goal here is to capture the reasoning chain and proposed mitigations so product/ops can triage risk vs gain.

Appendix (commands used):
- perf record: `perf record -F 99 -g -p <pid> -- sleep 120`
- py-spy: `py-spy record -o profile.svg --native --pid <pid> --duration 120`
- off-CPU (bcc): `python /usr/share/bcc/tools/offcputime -p <pid> 2>/dev/null | stackcollapse.pl > out.folded`

End of note.
